lessons.title: Measuring pasture and planning grazing
lessons.html:
The weekly farm walk

In this practical module you will manage pasture on a dairy: measure it, allocate it, fertilise and irrigate it, and plan renewal. The core activity is a regular farm walk, usually weekly.

Doing a pasture walk

  1. Walk every camp on the same route each week.
  2. Take readings with a calibrated rising plate meter or estimate cover in kg DM/ha with a method calibrated against cut samples.
  3. Record cover per camp, plus notes on weeds, pests, clover content, treading damage and leaf stage.
  4. Enter data into a spreadsheet or pasture software.

Building a feed wedge

Sort camps from highest to lowest cover and draw them as bars. Draw a target line from the planned pre-grazing cover down to the planned residual. Camps above the line indicate surplus; camps below indicate deficit.

  • Surplus: speed up the rotation or take surplus camps out for silage or hay.
  • Deficit: slow the rotation, increase supplements, apply nitrogen if growth conditions allow.

Calculating allocation

Example: 380 cows need 14 kg DM/cow/day from pasture = 5 320 kg DM. A camp of 3.5 ha has 2 900 kg DM/ha; target residual 1 500 kg DM/ha. Available = 1 400 × 3.5 = 4 900 kg DM. This camp is not enough for a full day; add 0.3 ha from the next camp, or supplement with about 420 kg DM.

Setting rotation length

Rotation length (days) = total grazing area ÷ area grazed per day. Example: 120 ha ÷ 4 ha per day = 30 days. Adjust according to growth rate and leaf stage; in fast spring growth the rotation may be shortened, in winter lengthened.

Instructing staff

Give the team written daily allocations: camp, area or strip size, back fence position, and times. Check residuals after grazing and give feedback.

lessons.title: Fertilising and irrigating pasture
lessons.html:
Soil sampling

  1. Divide the farm into management units of similar soil and use.
  2. Take many small cores at a consistent depth in a zig-zag pattern across each unit, avoiding dung pats, gateways and troughs.
  3. Mix, bag and label the sample; send to an accredited soil laboratory.
  4. Use the results for pH, phosphorus, potassium and other nutrients to plan lime and fertiliser with an agronomist.

Fertiliser programme

  • Apply lime well ahead of need, as it acts slowly.
  • Split nitrogen into regular applications matched to growth; avoid applying in cold dormancy or drought.
  • Account for nutrients in effluent and manure.
  • Calibrate spreaders so the actual rate matches the plan.
  • Keep buffer zones away from rivers and wetlands; avoid applying before heavy rain.
  • Record product, rate, camp and date.

Fertilisers fall under Act 36 of 1947. Store them away from feed and fuel.

Effluent irrigation

Apply dairy effluent only to designated lands, at rates and times consistent with the farm's water use authorisation under the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Rotate application areas and monitor soil nutrient levels to avoid build-up.

Irrigation scheduling

  • Use soil moisture probes, tensiometers or weather-based evapotranspiration data.
  • Irrigate to refill the root zone without causing runoff or deep drainage.
  • Check pivot nozzles, pressure and speed settings; repair leaks.
  • Record water applied and compare with the farm's water allocation.
  • Monitor electricity costs; schedule pumping outside peak tariff times where possible.

Safety

Wear gloves and dust masks when handling fertiliser and lime. Keep clear of moving pivots and power take-off shafts on spreaders, and switch off and remove keys before clearing blockages.

lessons.title: Pasture renewal, weeds and evaluation
lessons.html:
Planning pasture renewal

Rank camps by performance using grazing records (grazings per year, kg DM grown), botanical composition and weed levels. Renew the poorest camps first.

Establishment steps

  1. Correct soil pH and fertility from soil tests.
  2. Control weeds before planting.
  3. Choose species and cultivars suited to the site and feed plan, for example oversowing ryegrass into kikuyu in autumn, or establishing perennial ryegrass and clover under irrigation.
  4. Prepare the seedbed or use direct drilling to conserve soil and moisture.
  5. Sow at the recommended rate and depth; roll if appropriate for good seed-soil contact.
  6. Graze new pasture lightly once plants are well anchored (they should not pull out when tugged).

Weed and pest control

  • Prevent weeds through dense, well-grazed pasture and good fertility.
  • Identify problem weeds and declared weeds; the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 requires control of declared weeds and invader plants.
  • Use registered herbicides and pesticides only according to the label, by trained operators wearing the protective equipment specified.
  • Observe grazing withholding periods on the label before animals graze treated pasture.
  • Watch for pests such as army worm and cutworm, and act early.

Evaluating pasture performance

MeasureHow
Pasture grown (t DM/ha/year)Sum of growth from weekly walks
Pasture eatenPre-grazing minus residual, times area
Milk from pastureTotal milk minus milk attributable to supplements
Cost per kg DMAll pasture costs ÷ kg DM eaten

Compare the cost per kg DM of pasture with silage and purchased feeds to guide the feed strategy.

Key points

  • Walk and measure pasture weekly, and use a feed wedge to manage surplus and deficit.
  • Calculate daily allocations from cow demand and available DM.
  • Base fertiliser and lime on soil tests and record every application.
  • Schedule irrigation from soil moisture data and stay within water entitlements.
  • Renew the poorest camps first and control weeds by label and law.
